item.title: Domestic crude supply to refineries declines 6.3% to 15.97mb —NMDPRA
item.description: By Obas Esiedesa Domestic crude oil supply to Nigerian refineries declined by 6.3 per cent to 15.97 million barrels in September 2026 from 17.05 million barrels in August. This comes as petrol supply from domestic refineries and imports fell sharply during the month. The September 2026 Midstream and Downstream Report released by the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) on Thursday shows that the decline in crude supply coincided with a 23.4 per cent drop in average daily petrol supply to 38.7 million litres from 50.5 million litres in August. The report attributed the fall in petrol receipts to lower domestic supply and reduced imports as approved import permit volumes were being exhausted. Between January and September 2026, refineries received a combined 156.51 million barrels of crude oil, comprising 125.85 million barrels of domestic crude and 30.66 million barrels of imported crude. Domestic production accounted for 80.4 per cent of total intake, while imported cargoes contributed 19.6 per cent. The report further showed that Dangote Refinery’s utilisation stood at 105.98 per cent in September, implying crude processing of approximately 689,000 barrels per day against average crude receipts of 618,000 barrels per day. The difference of about 71,000 barrels per day was drawn from refinery inventory, indicating that the refinery processed more crude than it received during the month. Despite the September decline, domestic refineries remained the larger source of petrol supply, accounting for approximately 73.6 per cent of total receipts during the month, compared with 26.4 per cent from imports. The September total was also below the 13-month average of 49.7 million litres per day recorded between September 2025 and September 2026. Over the 13-month period, domestic refineries supplied an average of 30.4 million litres per day, accounting for 61.2 per cent of total supply, while imports contributed 19.3 million litres per day, or 38.8 per cent. The NMDPRA said September petrol receipts declined as domestic supply fell 21 per cent below August levels, while imports dropped by 30 per cent amid the exhaustion of approved import permit volumes. item.title: Stock market extend losses, 55 stocks depreciate
item.description: …As 20 record capital gains By Peter Egwuatu Share prices of 55 companies listed on the Nigerian Exchange Limited (NGX) depreciated last week following profit taking by the investors. However, 20 stocks appreciated in price during the week under review. The week’s performance highlights the market correction facing the stock market as investors reassess their portfolios following the substantial gains recorded earlier in the year. Although selected stocks attracted buying interest, the recovery was not broad enough to offset losses in influential stocks, leaving the overall market sentiment negative. Analysts emphasised that the decline also came against the backdrop of rising international oil prices, which climbed sharply amid escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. While higher crude prices could support Nigeria’s export earnings and government revenue, their broader implications for domestic fuel costs, inflation and business expenses remain important considerations for investors. A review of the market performance last week showed that the NGX market capitalisation, which represents the total value of stocks, shed over N206 billion to close at N160.519 trillion from N160.725 trillion the previous week. In similar manner, the NGX All Share Index, ASI, close lower to 247,222.27 points from 247539.73 points. Meanwhile, a total turnover of 2.024 billion shares worth N110.773 billion in 173,113 deals was traded last week by investors on the floor of the Exchange, in contrast to a total of 1.659 billion shares valued at N98.088 billion that exchanged hands the previous week in 184,632 deals. The Financial Services Industry (measured by volume) led the activity chart with 1.111 billion shares valued at N53.908 billion traded in 81,787 deals: thus contributing 54.89% and 48.66% to the total equity turnover volume and value respectively. The Consumer Goods Industry followed with 394.039 million shares worth N9.811 billion in 17,912 deals. Third place was the Agriculture Industry, with a turnover of 147.170 million shares worth N2.821 billion in 7,462 deals. Analysing market performance and outlook, analysts at InvestData Consulting Limited, stated: “The near-term outlook for the Nigerian equities market remains cautious as investors balance the need to preserve gains against opportunities in selected stocks. The market’s substantial year-to-date appreciation provides important context for the recent weakness, as some participants may be reducing exposure after the strong returns accumulated earlier in the year. Continued selling pressure in banking, energy and other influential stocks could prolong the market’s consolidation. Further weakness in large capitalised stocks may continue to weigh on the benchmark even if selected equities record positive returns.” The post Stock market extend losses, 55 stocks depreciate appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Soldiers earn peanuts, APC youth leader flaunts billion-naira SUVs — Utomi
item.description: Professor Pat Utomi has criticised the All Progressives Congress (APC) over the distribution of luxury sport utility vehicles (SUVs) to selected youth leaders, contrasting the expenditure with what he described as poor salaries paid to Nigerian soldiers. Utomi, a chieftain of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), said it was troubling that an APC youth leader could display expensive vehicles at a time Nigerians had been told that government funds were limited. In a post on X on Sunday, Utomi wrote: “Nigerian soldiers are being paid peanuts as salaries, yet an APC youth leader is flaunting SUVs worth billions of naira. This is the same government that told Nigerians there was no longer money in the treasury. At this point, they must think we are fools!” In another post, the professor questioned whether the money spent on the vehicles could have been put to better use, particularly in the health sector. “Each of the SUVs in this video costs more than ₦100 million. I wonder how many world-class ambulances the millions being spent on these vehicles could buy. What a pity!” he wrote. The comments followed a video posted by APC National Youth Leader, Dayo Israel, showing brand-new 2026 Toyota Prado SUVs he said were presented to selected youth leaders to support election mobilisation ahead of the 2027 general elections. “Today, I presented brand new 2026 Prado to my committed selected youth leaders to aid their election mobilisation activities,” Israel wrote. He also expressed gratitude to First Lady Oluremi Tinubu for what he described as her continued support for the party’s structure under his leadership. “The party is supreme and that supremacy will show in our action in this election period — we will deliver polling unit by polling unit,” he added. The video, which has since been deleted, drew criticism from Nigerians on social media, with some questioning the timing of the vehicle distribution amid the economic hardship associated with the Tinubu administration’s reforms. Utomi’s remarks add to the criticism surrounding the display, with the NDC chieftain raising questions about public spending priorities and the cost of the vehicles. It said the dialogue should include Miyetti Allah groups, traditional rulers, the Christian Association of Nigeria CAN, Jama’atu Nasril Islam JNI, security agencies and state governments, with a mandate of “Truth, Justice, Forgiveness, Compensation, and a Roadmap for Peaceful Co-existence.” The groups also listed responsibilities for pastoralist communities, urging leaders, households and young people to respect farmers’ rights and lawful property, take “reasonable measures to prevent livestock from entering cultivated farmland”, and cooperate with lawful security investigations. item.title: IPoB alleges secret transfer of 68 detainees
item.description: By Steve Oko UMUAHIA—The Indigenous People of Biafra, IPoB, has alleged that 68 detained Biafrans were secretly transferred from Wawa Barracks to correctional facilities in Kuje, Keffi and Suleja, accusing the Federal Government of using the justice system to prolong the detention of its members. The group also alleged that the Court of Appeal had yet to list an appeal challenging the conviction of its leader, Mazi Nnamdi Kanu, despite the compilation and transmission of the record of appeal. IPOB made the allegations in its weekly address issued on Sunday by the Head of its Directorate of State, DOS, Mazi Chris Nwaogu. Nwaogu said the group’s legal team had identified the 68 detainees and was working to secure their release. He urged supporters to sustain legal efforts on behalf of those in custody. He further alleged that a separate fundamental rights suit concerning Kanu’s detention had suffered a setback after the presiding judge reportedly announced that the court file was missing. According to him, the suit concerns Kanu’s detention for 14 months following his discharge by the Court of Appeal on October 13, 2022. The IPOB spokesman also challenged the legal basis of Kanu’s conviction by Justice Omotosho on November 20, 2025, alleging that the judgment relied on a repealed law. He cited Section 36(12) of the Constitution, which provides that a person cannot be convicted of a criminal offence unless the offence and its penalty are prescribed in written law. Meanwhile, IPOB disowned an audio message circulating online that purportedly announced the return of an enforced Monday sit-at-home across the South-East. Nwaọgụ said neither the DOS nor the High Command of the Eastern Security Network, ESN, had authorised the action, warning against attempts to enforce an unauthorised shutdown. He urged residents to disregard the message and avoid actions capable of provoking violence or disrupting economic activities in the region. The group also announced what it described as a phased political disengagement, directing its supporters to boycott activities associated with the All Progressives Congress, APC, ahead of the 2027 general elections. It urged supporters to stay away from APC rallies, stop carrying the party’s flags and refrain from defending APC governors, while maintaining its position on boycotting the 2027 elections. Nwaọgụ said the proposed boycott was a response to what the group described as injustice, unlawful detention and persecution of its members. He, however, cautioned supporters against violence and warned politicians against hijacking the planned boycott for their own interests. IPOB reiterated its demand for Kanu’s immediate and unconditional release, urging the judiciary to list the appeal for hearing and determine the legal issues surrounding his conviction. item.title: Stock market extend losses, 55 stocks depreciate; 20 record capital gains
item.description: By Peter Egwuatu Share prices of 55 companies listed on the Nigerian Exchange Limited (NGX) depreciated last week following profit taking by the investors. However, 20 stocks appreciated in price during the week under review. The week’s performance highlights the market correction facing the stock market as investors reassess their portfolios following the substantial gains recorded earlier in the year. Although selected stocks attracted buying interest, the recovery was not broad enough to offset losses in influential stocks, leaving the overall market sentiment negative. Analysts emphasised that the decline also came against the backdrop of rising international oil prices, which climbed sharply amid escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. While higher crude prices could support Nigeria’s export earnings and government revenue, their broader implications for domestic fuel costs, inflation and business expenses remain important considerations for investors. A review of the market performance last week showed that the NGX market capitalisation, which represents the total value of stocks, shed over N206 billion to close at N160.519 trillion from N160.725 trillion the previous week. In similar manner, the NGX All Share Index, ASI, close lower to 247,222.27 points from 247539.73 points. Meanwhile, a total turnover of 2.024 billion shares worth N110.773 billion in 173,113 deals was traded last week by investors on the floor of the Exchange, in contrast to a total of 1.659 billion shares valued at N98.088 billion that exchanged hands the previous week in 184,632 deals. The Financial Services Industry (measured by volume) led the activity chart with 1.111 billion shares valued at N53.908 billion traded in 81,787 deals: thus contributing 54.89% and 48.66% to the total equity turnover volume and value respectively. The Consumer Goods Industry followed with 394.039 million shares worth N9.811 billion in 17,912 deals. Third place was the Agriculture Industry, with a turnover of 147.170 million shares worth N2.821 billion in 7,462 deals. Analysing market performance and outlook, analysts at InvestData Consulting Limited, stated: “The near-term outlook for the Nigerian equities market remains cautious as investors balance the need to preserve gains against opportunities in selected stocks. The market’s substantial year-to-date appreciation provides important context for the recent weakness, as some participants may be reducing exposure after the strong returns accumulated earlier in the year. Continued selling pressure in banking, energy and other influential stocks could prolong the market’s consolidation. Further weakness in large capitalised stocks may continue to weigh on the benchmark even if selected equities record positive returns.” Vanguard News The post Stock market extend losses, 55 stocks depreciate; 20 record capital gains appeared first on Vanguard News .

He urged Nigerians contacted by public health officials to cooperate fully and provide accurate information about their movements, contacts and any symptoms they might have experienced. He added that genetic sequencing had been completed by two laboratory facilities to establish the genetic characteristics of the virus, with the findings being used to facilitate information-sharing with Ugandan health authorities. item.title: Death toll in Taraba bandits’ attack now 50
item.description: The death toll from an attack by gunmen in Taraba State has risen to at least 50, survivors and Amnesty International told AFP Sunday, after more bodies were discovered. Read Also: ‘We counted over 20 bodies after attackers left’ – Taraba massacre survivors Both police and Amnesty said some of the victims had drowned while trying to flee the attackers. Gunmen on motorcycles from a suspected “bandit” gang swarmed Binnari, in eastern Taraba, killing dozens of people shortly after Friday prayers. They also looted and burned stores. Taraba is sandwiched between northeastern Nigeria, which has a long-running jihadist insurgency, and the volatile central region, which faces criminal gangs known as bandits. Driven by money rather than ideology, the bandits in Nigeria target poorly policed rural areas, kidnapping for ransom and killing. “On Friday, we found seven bodies after the bandits attacked our community,” said Bashir Mamuda Musa, a resident of Binnari, in Taraba state. “The following day, Saturday, we discovered another 43 bodies in the river, bringing the total to 50,” he added. The new toll was confirmed by resident Abdullahi Zakari. “Many residents, including women and children, fled towards the river in an attempt to escape the gunmen,” Zakari told AFP. “Unfortunately, several people drowned while trying to flee the attack.” ‘Chased into river’ Bodies can often be difficult to recover when communities scatter. Some were discovered in a nearby river, according to both police and Amnesty. Police spokesman for the state Victor Msheliza told AFP on Sunday that they were still searching the area. Officers “found some (bodies) in the river” of people who were trying to escape, he said. Police were immediately deployed to the area after the attack, more deployments being sent, he said. Amnesty International gave a toll of 52 on Sunday, saying the attackers had come “in large numbers and set ablaze shops and market stalls”. “The bandits invaded in large numbers,… chased people and they headed toward the river to escape,” and drowned, Amnesty International Nigeria director Isa Sanusi told AFP. “Some were chased into the river by the gunmen”. Banditry has become a growing problem in northwest and central Nigeria, with powerful gangs battling overstretched police and military across hard-to-reach, rural locations. They raid villages and impose “taxes” on farmers and mining operations in areas with little state presence. Amnesty, in a post on X, blamed the Nigerian authorities for leaving some rural communities “at the mercy of gunmen that repeatedly commit atrocities with impunity. “Consistent failure of the authorities to bring the suspected perpetrators to justice is clearly emboldening impunity,” the rights group said on social media. item.title: Kane primed to beat Yamal, Mbappe to Ballon d’Or glory
item.description: England captain Harry Kane is the favourite to win a wide open race to be crowned Ballon d’Or winner at a glitzy London ceremony on Monday, with Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe also in the running to be named the world’s best footballer. Read Also: 2026 Ballon d’or ceremony: date, time and how to watch The 70th edition of the award, established by the magazine France Football, will be hosted in England for the first time in recognition of the first winner Stanley Matthews and fittingly could have a first English winner for 25 years. Bayern Munich striker Kane struck a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for club and country last season, leading the German giants to a league and cup double and England to the semi-finals of the World Cup. “I’d love to be able to achieve something like that. I would be a massive milestone in my career,” said the 33-year-old. But semi-final exits in both the Champions League and World Cup for Kane means the outcome is far from certain. “I think my wife would prefer to know and my family … it’s very stressful for everyone,” he added. “I can see why they don’t tell people. They want everyone to go, all the big names, and there will be more people watching it if they don’t know.” ‘I deserve it’ Yamal finished second to Paris Saint-Germain’s Ousmane Dembele last year and the 19-year-old Barcelona superstar seems destined to be a Ballon d’Or winner one day. However, after a hamstring injury ended his club season early, he was far from the shining light of Spain’s World Cup triumph that was built on being the best collective unit. Yamal was pipped to both the player and young player of the tournament by his Barcelona team-mates Rodri and Pau Cubarsi. That has not diminished his bullish confidence ahead of the ceremony. “For me, Mbappe and me, we’re the two best players in the world,” Yamal said last month. “I honestly think that, as the best in the world, maybe there are two of us, and this year I would deserve it because of what I’ve won.” Mbappe, by contrast, boasts plenty of personal milestones without medals for either Real Madrid or France. The 27-year-old was top goalscorer in La Liga, the Champions League and the World Cup without winning any of those trophies. His 10 World Cup goals made him the top goalscorer in the competition’s history on 22. “Being the all-time top scorer in World Cup history, overtaking all the great legends in the history of the sport in the most important tournament there is, is something that really stands out,” said Mbappe. “Who am I voting for? Myself.” One football journalist from each of the 100 top nations in FIFA’s rankings is invited to cast votes for their top 10 players from a 30-man shortlist, allocating a maximum of 15 points down to one based on their ranking. The Ballon d’Or goes to the player who accrued the most points. Although the award carries no cash prize, it can generate huge bonuses from clubs and commercial partners as well as increasing a player’s overall marketing value.

His re-election marks another remarkable comeback for the man who grew up dirt poor in the northeast in a family of illiterate farmers. Lula, revered for social welfare programs that lifted millions out of poverty, made a dramatic return to office in 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months. item.description: By ANTHONY OGBEIFUN As Nigeria approaches the 2027 general election, the country stands again at a familiar crossroads: the choice between narrow, sectional calculation and the broader national demand for justice, fairness and peace. Elections are not merely contests for power. In a plural society such as Nigeria, they are also referendums on whether citizens believe the state belongs to all of them. Few Nigerian voices expressed this truth more memorably than the late elder statesman and Dan Masanin Kano, Alhaji Yusuf Maitama Sule. In May 2015, Sule led a delegation of the Northern Leaders Forum to congratulate then President-elect Muhammadu Buhari. His counsel on that occasion remains strikingly relevant today. Sule told Buhari: “With justice, you can rule Nigeria well. Justice is the key.” It was a simple statement, but one carrying the weight of Nigeria’s history. The country’s recurrent crises—ethnic suspicion, religious tension, electoral violence, insecurity, economic exclusion and the erosion of public trust—are not disconnected accidents. They are symptoms of a deeper disorder: the feeling among many citizens that fairness is selective, opportunity is unequal and power is used to reward loyalty rather than serve the common good. Sule understood this. “Behind every crisis anywhere in the world is injustice,” he said. And the antidote, he insisted, is “justice.” That insight should guide every political party, candidate, campaign organisation and voter ahead of 2027. What conquers is the spirit and the weapons of governing the mind and conquering the spirit are justice and fair play.” Nigeria’s 2027 election will therefore test not only the popularity of candidates, but the moral seriousness of the political class. Justice, in the sense Sule meant it, is broader than court judgments or legal technicalities. It includes fair representation, equitable distribution of public resources, respect for the rule of law, protection of minorities, credible elections and equal treatment before public institutions. It means that a farmer in Zamfara, a trader in Onitsha, a teacher in Lagos, a fisherman in Bayelsa and a herder in Sokoto should all be able to expect the state to protect their lives, respect their rights and respond to their needs without discrimination. Sule put it plainly: “If you do justice to all and sundry — and I say all and sundry — because Allah says, ‘If you are going to judge between two people, do justice irrespective of the tribe, religion or even political inclination; justice must be done to whosoever deserves it.’” That standard is demanding. It rejects the politics of “our turn” when it becomes a cover for exclusion. It also rejects the politics of revenge, where one group’s victory is treated as another group’s defeat. Nigeria needs leaders who can rise above such thinking. The late Dan Masanin Kano was equally clear that justice must not be selective. “I am not asking you — and I know you will not — to discriminate against any part of Nigeria,” he told Buhari. “But I am asking you to do justice to all parts of Nigeria.” For political parties preparing for 2027, fairness must begin before the first ballot is cast. It must be visible in candidate selection, zoning arrangements, internal party democracy, campaign financing and the treatment of aspirants. When parties manipulate primaries, impose candidates, marginalise women and young people, or allow money to determine nomination, they weaken the legitimacy of the eventual winner. A flawed process produces a fragile mandate. And a fragile mandate makes governing harder, especially in a country where citizens are already sceptical of political promises. Fairness also requires issue-based campaigns. Nigeria’s problems are real: insecurity, unemployment, inflation, poor infrastructure, weak public services, climate pressure on agriculture and widespread poverty. These challenges do not respect ethnicity or religion. Candidates should therefore be judged on their plans to secure communities, create jobs, reform institutions, expand opportunities and restore public confidence. Sule linked justice directly to peace and development. “Justice will bring about peace,” he said. “Peace and stability are the pre-requisites of development.” No society develops sustainably in an atmosphere of fear. Investors hesitate where contracts are uncertain and violence is common. Farmers abandon land where insecurity prevails. Young people lose hope where merit is ignored and corruption rewards the connected. Communities retreat into distrust when they believe the state protects some citizens more than others. Peace is not merely the absence of gunfire. It is the presence of confidence: confidence that elections will count, that courts will be impartial, that public offices will serve the public, and that no region, faith or class will be permanently shut out of opportunity. The 2027 election offers Nigeria a chance to rebuild that confidence. But it will require more than campaign rhetoric. It will require electoral institutions that are visibly independent, security agencies that act professionally, political actors who accept results peacefully, and citizens who refuse to be used as instruments of violence. Nigeria does not lack talent, resources or ideas. What it often lacks is the disciplined commitment to justice that turns diversity into strength rather than division. Maitama Sule’s message was not addressed to one president alone. It was addressed to every Nigerian leader, in every generation, and to every citizen who hopes for a better country. As 2027 approaches, voters should ask hard questions: Which candidate will uphold the rule of law even when it is inconvenient? Which party will distribute opportunity fairly? It should be based on justice. Sule’s counsel remains a compass: “With justice, you can rule Nigeria well. Justice is the key.” If Nigeria’s political class embraces that key, the 2027 election can become more than another contest for office. It can become a renewal of the national promise—a step towards a country at peace with itself, fair to all its people, and capable at last of fulfilling its vast potential. •Ogbeifun wrote in from Lagos. item.title: Making gas operations safer
item.description: Nigeria’s ambition to expand the use of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) must be matched by a serious commitment to safety. The Nigerian Association of Liquefied Petroleum Gas Marketers (NALPGAM), at its recent webinar on operational excellence and compliance, warned that rising consumption alone cannot guarantee a sustainable industry. Every facility must be safe, every operator competent, every process compliant and every customer protected. The warning is timely. LPG offers households and businesses a cleaner alternative to firewood, charcoal and other polluting fuels, but it is highly flammable. Leaking gas, overfilled cylinders, defective valves, poorly maintained equipment and unsafe storage can turn premises into disaster scenes. Illegal decanting and unauthorised propane blending compound these risks, endangering workers, consumers and neighbouring communities. Such practices must not be treated as commercial shortcuts. NALPGAM’s proposed Standard of Operational Excellence, built around safe facilities, trained personnel, compliant processes and consumer protection, deserves support. But a declaration is not enforcement. The association must translate its aspiration into measurable obligations for members, while the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) must sustain inspections, investigate violations and apply sanctions. Operators should maintain equipment, verify cylinder integrity, provide fire and gas-detection systems, and report incidents promptly. Regulators should publish inspection and enforcement data so the public can judge progress. Technology can strengthen this effort. Smart filling systems, calibrated load cells, flow meters, automated tank gauges and vehicle tracking can improve measurement, trace product movements and expose losses or suspicious transactions. Digital tools, however, are no substitute for trained staff, independent checks and functioning emergency procedures. Small operators may need affordable training, technical guidance and finance for compliant upgrades; such assistance must never become an excuse to relax minimum safety standards. Safety also has an economic dimension. Accidents destroy lives, property, investment and public confidence. item.content:encoded: Nigeria’s ambition to expand the use of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) must be matched by a serious commitment to safety. The Nigerian Association of Liquefied Petroleum Gas Marketers (NALPGAM), at its recent webinar on operational excellence and compliance, warned that rising consumption alone cannot guarantee a sustainable industry. Every facility must be safe, every operator competent, every process compliant and every customer protected. The warning is timely. LPG offers households and businesses a cleaner alternative to firewood, charcoal and other polluting fuels, but it is highly flammable. Leaking gas, overfilled cylinders, defective valves, poorly maintained equipment and unsafe storage can turn premises into disaster scenes. Illegal decanting and unauthorised propane blending compound these risks, endangering workers, consumers and neighbouring communities. Such practices must not be treated as commercial shortcuts. NALPGAM’s proposed Standard of Operational Excellence, built around safe facilities, trained personnel, compliant processes and consumer protection, deserves support. But a declaration is not enforcement. The association must translate its aspiration into measurable obligations for members, while the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) must sustain inspections, investigate violations and apply sanctions. Operators should maintain equipment, verify cylinder integrity, provide fire and gas-detection systems, and report incidents promptly. Regulators should publish inspection and enforcement data so the public can judge progress. Technology can strengthen this effort. Smart filling systems, calibrated load cells, flow meters, automated tank gauges and vehicle tracking can improve measurement, trace product movements and expose losses or suspicious transactions. Digital tools, however, are no substitute for trained staff, independent checks and functioning emergency procedures. Small operators may need affordable training, technical guidance and finance for compliant upgrades; such assistance must never become an excuse to relax minimum safety standards. Safety also has an economic dimension. Accidents destroy lives, property, investment and public confidence. Consumers who fear explosions or suspect short-changing may avoid cooking gas, frustrating efforts to broaden its use. Reliable cylinder traceability, approved exchange arrangements, accurate measurement and clear consumer information can build trust. Government should involve marketers in LPG penetration and cylinder recirculation programmes, while improving supply and distribution infrastructure to make fuel more accessible and affordable. The stakes extend beyond individual kitchens. Wider adoption of LPG can reduce household exposure to smoke from solid fuels and ease pressure on forests. A safer, better-regulated market can also attract investment, support certified local cylinder manufacturing, create jobs and deepen Nigeria’s energy economy. The national target of five million tonnes of annual LPG consumption by 2030 will mean little if expansion outpaces safety capacity. Government, regulators and marketers must turn promises into deadlines, audits, transparent reporting and consequences for negligence. Safety must govern every delivery, filling and transaction. Only then can Nigerians embrace gas with confidence, the environment benefit, and the industry become a pillar of economic diversification. Unexplained bleeding or bruising may occur in some cases. “As early symptoms can resemble malaria and other common illnesses, residents who become unwell, particularly after possible exposure or travel from an area with active transmission, should seek prompt medical assessment,” it added. State’s fever-management policy. “Where the test is negative, a healthcare professional should assess other possible causes and determine appropriate treatment,” it said. “Residents are also advised to wash their hands regularly, avoid contact with the body fluids of sick persons, refrain from handling potentially contaminated materials and avoid contact with sick or dead wild animals.” health information when requested, and comply with applicable public health guidance. “Anyone who develops symptoms during travel or after arrival should promptly notify the appropriate health personnel and seek guidance before visiting a healthcare facility,” it added. “Airlines and airport operators are expected to sustain established public health protocols, while travellers should consult official advisories from the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), the Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) and the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN) for current guidance.” The state government urged anyone who suspects exposure to Ebola, especially following contact with a suspected or confirmed case, to promptly contact public health authorities for guidance before visiting a healthcare facility. “Suspected cases or relevant exposure concerns in Lagos may be reported through the State’s emergency numbers, 112 or 767, or to the Directorate of response readiness, coordinate with relevant stakeholders and provide verified updates as necessary. Residents are encouraged to remain calm, practise recommended preventive measures and follow official public health announcements. Early detection and prompt reporting save lives.” The post Ebola: Lagos Intensifies Surveillance, Reassures Residents Of Preparedness appeared first on Channels Television .

item.title: Opebi-Mende-Ojota Link Bridge To Be Opened Before Christmas, Says Sanwo-Olu
item.description: The Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu has said that the Opebi-Mende Link Bridge is about 80 per cent complete, expressing confidence that the project will be opened to the public before Christmas. Governor Sanwo-Olu gave the assurance during an inspection of the project, acknowledging that the construction had exceeded the September completion timeline previously announced. He said his visit to the site was to establish the reasons for the delay and assess the progress of work, stressing that the project’s distinctive architectural design and engineering requirements must not be compromised by the pressure to meet the deadline. He explained that the bridge’s steel structure was designed to reflect the area’s historical association with cane weaving, thereby preserving its cultural identity. According to him, the project involves installing more than 300 tonnes of steel at heights of up to 25 metres, making it an unusually demanding engineering undertaking. The governor said three of the four major steel components, designed to resemble interwoven cane, had been completed, while work was ongoing on the remaining component. He added that light-emitting diode (LED) installations featuring the colours of Lagos State would enhance the structure and give it an iconic appearance. Governor Sanwo-Olu added that the state government would not sacrifice engineering quality and public safety for speed, despite the delay. He said additional activities, including site cleaning, repainting of kerbs, restoration of affected areas and landscaping, would be undertaken before the bridge is opened to the public. He envisaged the area becoming a destination for recreation, cultural heritage and tourism, adding that its redevelopment would enable residents to appreciate the history and identity of the community. The governor maintained that the bridge would become a significant infrastructure landmark in Lagos, combining innovation with cultural preservation. Sanwo-Olu commissioned the construction of the bridge in 2022 to ease congestion in Ikeja and environs. Governor Sanwo-Olu (centre) He said that the bridge, which is part of the ‘legacy project,’ was an innovative solution to the perennial gridlock around Opebi/Mobolaji Bank Anthony Way/Ojota/Mende corridor. item.title: Were Young People Removed From Nigeria’s Voter Register?
item.description: The recent voter registration figures released by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) have raised important questions about the declining number of young people on Nigeria’s voter register. The 2026 age distribution is as follows: • Youth: 18–34 years: 29,777,578 (28.79 per cent) • Middle age: 35–49 years: 43,265,946 (41.83 per cent) • Elderly: 50–69 years: 22,982,900 (22.22 per cent) • 70 years and above: 7,402,291 (7.16 per cent) What Do These Figures Tell Us? 1. Their share of the register also declined from 39.6 per cent in 2023 to 28.79 per cent in 2026, a decrease of approximately 10.9 percentage points. 2. item.title: Police Foil Railway Vandalism, Arrest Four Suspects With 70 Stolen Sleepers In Katsina
item.description: The Katsina State Police Command has arrested four suspected railway vandals and recovered 70 railway sleepers believed to have been stolen. The suspects were apprehended on October 11, 2026, at about 12:30 a.m., when police operatives on routine stop-and-search duty along the Kurfi–Tsanni Village Road intercepted a white J5 vehicle. The vehicle, driven by a 25-year-old man, was said to be carrying three other occupants. A thorough search of the vehicle uncovered 70 railway sleepers carefully concealed behind 17 bags of animal feed in what investigators believe was an attempt to evade detection. Police said preliminary investigations revealed that one of the suspects confessed to receiving the railway materials from a suspected supplier from Bauchi State, who is currently at large. The police said 70 railway sleepers were carefully concealed behind 17 bags of animal feed in what investigators believe was an attempt to evade detection. According to the police command, the stolen items were being transported for delivery to a man in Katsina. It said that the four suspects are currently in police custody, while the operational vehicle, the recovered railway sleepers and the bags of animal feed used to conceal them have been secured as exhibits. The Command said efforts are underway to apprehend the fleeing suspects and determine the exact location from which the railway infrastructure was vandalised, adding that investigations are ongoing. In a statement issued on Sunday, the Police Public Relations Officer, DSP Abubakar Sadiq, described the arrests as another breakthrough in the fight against crimes targeting critical national infrastructure. Sadiq said the Commissioner of Police, CP Ali Umar Fage, reaffirmed the Command’s unwavering commitment to protecting critical national infrastructure and bringing perpetrators of vandalism to justice. The PPRO said that the commissioner also appealed to residents to continue supporting security agencies with timely and credible information that will enable the police to prevent crime and swiftly apprehend criminal elements across the state.
